Our contrastive partition reward (Contrastive) shows a positive lag-1 trend (ρ=+0.077\rho=+0.077, 95% CI [+0.007,+0.123][+0.007,+0.123], n=1,136n=1{,}136, raw permutation p=0.04p=0.04) that is not significant after Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the 7-lag family (q=0.28q=0.28) but FDR-significant on the underlying surprisal score (ρ=+0.131\rho=+0.131, q=0.046q=0.046). The Contrastive trend on surprisal decays monotonically toward zero by lag 4, consistent with local inheritance. The baseline shows no such decay structure on either metric. See Figure 6.

We note that the Contrastive correlation is consistent with two mechanisms our analysis cannot uniquely distinguish: (a) inheritable signal in the score itself, exploitable by UCT-selection; or (b) a downstream effect of the structured MM-cell partition being available as ancestor context to the next-level proposer, which would correlate child and parent scores through generation rather than through selection. The natural ablation, comparing UCT-selection to uniform-random parent selection while preserving context inheritance, would adjudicate (a) vs. (b) and is left to future work.

Appendix I Blinded Expert Evaluation

This appendix gives the protocol, reliability, and control analyses behind Table 1.

Protocol.

Thirty-eight evaluators with MS or PhD degrees in the mathematical, computational, or natural sciences, recruited and screened separately from the authors (31 through a screened crowd platform, 7 verified in person), rated 60 blinded items: ten per dataset, stratified by the contrastive score κt\kappa_{t}. Each evaluator saw only the research question, the candidate explanations, and the statistical evidence from the executed analysis, with the alternatives in random order; our system’s beliefs, its resolution label, and the pointwise verdict were never shown. Each item was rated by at least 4 evaluators (median 8). The four questions per item were (Q1) which explanation the evidence supports, with the extra options “none of these is supported” and “cannot tell”; (Q2) whether the alternatives are mutually exclusive and cover the plausible explanations, with options for a missing explanation, overlap, or both; (Q3) whether the result is worth reporting; and (Q4) whether the chosen variables and test fit the question. We score items by majority vote and count no majority, “cannot tell,” and “none” as disagreement with our system’s explanation. Five submissions were excluded under a rule fixed at the first exclusion (one incomplete session and four evaluators who missed both attention checks). Restricting to the 30 evaluators who caught every attention check lowers the overall agreement from 71.7% to 68.3%, so inattentive raters do not carry the result. Expert evaluations were collected with informed consent and kept confidential; the information concerned our methods and scientific outputs, not the evaluators as individuals. Under our institution’s IRB guidance, this activity does not constitute human-subjects research and therefore did not require IRB review.

Both methods were compared on the same 60 questions, using the same evidence and expert judgments. The pointwise hypothesis was the explanation our system rated most plausible before seeing the evidence, evaluated on its own.

Resolution agreement (Q1).

The expert majority matched our system’s explanation on 43 of 60 items (71.7%, 95% CI 60.0–83.3 by item-clustered bootstrap): 40 of the 51 items it marked resolved (78.4%) and 3 of the 9 it left unresolved. Of the 17 disagreements, the experts chose a competing explanation on only 3; on 8 they judged the evidence insufficient and on 6 they formed no majority, so most disagreements fall on evidence the experts themselves could not settle. Across all 60 items the panel committed to a specific alternative on 46, which shows that the executed experiments usually separate the alternatives well enough for experts to commit. Agreement was 79% on confirmative resolutions and 77% on corrective ones. Against the pointwise baseline: on the 32 items it confirmed, the experts endorsed 23 findings for each method; on the 22 items it rejected and stopped, the alternative our system identified matched the expert majority on 18 (81.8%; exact 95% CI 60–95). A related subset, the 22 items the baseline did not confirm and our system resolved, overlaps this one on 19 items and gives 17 of 22; the main text reports the pointwise-rejected subset. Per dataset, agreement ranges from 6 of 10 to 9 of 10, too few items to compare domains.

Reliability.

On the load-bearing judgment (Q1, four to six options), pairwise agreement was 64% and Krippendorff’s α\alpha was 0.54 (95% CI 0.45–0.61), and in a descriptive stratification α\alpha was 0.60 on resolved items versus 0.22 on unresolved ones, so rater disagreement concentrates on the items Contrastive Discovery leaves unresolved. On set completeness (Q2), 80% of ratings judged the set well formed, 15% flagged a missing plausible alternative, 4% overlap, and 1% both; raw agreement on the binary omission call was 83% (Gwet’s AC1 =0.73=0.73; the lower Fleiss’ κ\kappa of 0.35 reflects the 80/20 response skew). A strict majority flagged a missing alternative on 6 of the 60 sets. Analysis appropriateness (Q4) was judged appropriate on 73% of ratings, wrong variable or test on 19%, and cannot tell on 8% (binary raw agreement 72%, AC1 =0.54=0.54). Scientific value (Q3) had low agreement (α=0.24\alpha=0.24), so we report it only as a distribution: 51% substantive finding, 20% minor, 3% too obvious to state, 25% not a finding.

Validity controls.

To check that the ratings track genuine quality, we planted two manually constructed defective sets among the items, one with a plausible alternative removed and one with overlapping alternatives: 11 of the 14 evaluators who saw the first flagged a missing alternative and none confused it with overlap, and 10 of 12 flagged the second as defective. On separate control items we kept the contrast set intact but paired it with the evidence of a different question: the well-formed rate stayed at 77%, close to its 80% baseline, while the analysis-appropriateness rating fell from 73% to 7% and the wrong-variable-or-test flag rose from 19% to 84%. The evaluators therefore flag real set defects without blanket-flagging, and recognize when an analysis does not fit its question. Attention controls (mismatched evidence expected to yield “cannot tell”) fired as expected on 95% of exposures.

Scope.

The experts read the same evidence as our system, so their agreement shows that resolutions track the evidence as independent experts read it; it is not a test of scientific truth. The experts were general quantitative-science raters rather than specialists matched to each item’s subfield, and they judged the executed analysis rather than replicating it. The comparison with the pointwise baseline is one of endorsed yield, not of accuracy on the items both methods decide.

Appendix J Mechanical Fidelity Audits

The belief step reads the analyst’s written summary of an executed analysis. Three audits, none of which involves a language model in the scoring, check that this chain is faithful: that the adjudication follows the evidence it is shown, that the summary reports the numbers the code printed, and that the code computed those numbers correctly.

Adjudication follows the evidence.

We took 14 claims from 10 DiscoveryBench training questions with documented findings (a finding with two claims contributes two), constructed contrast sets whose wording was held fixed across conditions, and ran the production posterior elicitor (gpt-4o-2024-08-06, five samples, τsupport=0.80\tau_{\mathrm{support}}=0.80) on numbers-only evidence with the alternatives in randomized order and no analyst prose. Given the full statistic with its interval, available for 11 of the 14, the elicitor placed the documented answer first in every case and resolved 8 of 11, holding back on three whose intervals lie close to zero. Given the coefficient without an interval it still ranked the documented answer first on 13 of 14 while resolving only 7, appropriate caution when the evidence is incomplete. In a separate condition covering all 14 claims, we supplied the statistic with its sign reversed; the resolution followed the reversal in every case. Supplying no evidence produced no resolution on any of the 14 (largest posterior 0.74). Because the wording of the alternatives was identical across the four conditions, these resolutions follow the evidence and not the phrasing. This establishes evidence-driven adjudication, not end-to-end correctness of the pipeline that produces the evidence.

Summaries quote the numbers the code printed.

Across all available seeds, 3,015 analyses contained checkable numerical claims in the analyst’s written summary. We checked, allowing for rounding, percentages, and scientific notation, whether those numbers appear in the captured standard output of the executed code. 99.1% of these analyses and 99.7% of the 9,239 checked numbers are grounded in a printed value. Reading every mismatch by hand found at least five genuine slips, including a slope quoted from a plot-only run and a count reported as a percentage; the audit caught all of them without a human in the loop. Pairing each summary with a different analysis’s output and re-running the identical matcher grounds only 3.8% of numbers, so the check discriminates. Signs are not checked by this audit.

The code computed the statistics correctly.

For the analyses whose statistic can be rebuilt directly from named columns of the raw data (400 of 3,274; 331 scorable, spanning every available seed and 251 distinct dataset/test/column combinations), we recomputed the statistic with standard libraries and compared it to the value the agent printed. The values matched on 318 of 331 (96.1%). Every mismatch we could trace came from our recomputation missing a data-handling step in the agent’s code (a custom parser, a missing-data rule, a −9999-9999 sentinel replaced before analysis, a group split); a few could not be classified either way. We found no confirmed computation error. Substituting a wrong column matches only 2.1% of the time, so the check is not loose. Coverage is 12% of analyses and not random, since the rebuildable analyses are the simpler ones, so we read this as a check on the covered analyses rather than a pipeline-wide rate.

Appendix K Handling Incomplete Contrast Sets

A contrast set that omits the explanation the evidence supports can produce a confident wrong resolution. We measured how often this happens and how well the abstention alternative of Section 3.4 prevents it.

Design.

We used two frozen panels. The primary panel is 163 questions, all directional triples (M=3M=3), whose supported explanation is fixed by a statistic recomputed from the raw data with no model in the scoring (121 distinct underlying analyses; intervals are clustered on the analysis). Because the correct answer must be present to be removed, this panel conditions on questions the system originally resolved correctly, so the intact-set control measures re-elicitation stability rather than corpus accuracy. A secondary panel is 40 resolved questions across six partition types and M∈{2,3,4}M\in\{2,3,4\} whose supported explanation matches the blinded expert majority of Appendix I. The design crossed two factors: the set as generated or with the supported explanation removed, each with or without an added alternative worded “none of the listed alternatives matches the evidence; the contrast set is incomplete.” The seven secondary-panel questions with M=2M=2 omitted the removed-explanation condition without the added alternative, since its sole survivor would receive all belief by construction. Selecting the added alternative flags the set as incomplete; declining to reach τsupport\tau_{\mathrm{support}} withholds resolution as before. Cell order was randomized per call and five samples were requested for aggregation before thresholding. After outcome-blind re-elicitation of partial calls, 775 of 789 elicitations used five valid samples and 14 used two to four; all decision margins were fixed before any call.

Results.

With the sets left intact, the supported explanation resolved on 159 of 163 questions (97.5%) without the abstention alternative and on 162 of 163 (99.4%) with it, and the abstention alternative was never selected (0 of 163). With the supported explanation removed (Table 10), the system resolved to a surviving alternative on 53.4% of questions, so an omitted explanation can indeed produce a wrong resolution. The failures lean toward caution: when a direction was removed and the null survived, the system resolved to “no detectable effect” on 58.5% of cases, left the question unresolved on 38.7%, and asserted the opposite direction on 2.8%; when the null was removed and only opposing directions survived, it left all 21 unresolved. Those null resolutions are still wrong under our reference, which is why the abstention alternative matters. The abstention alternative cuts false resolution to 0.6%: it is the leading option on 92.6% of removed cases (mean mass 0.85) and crosses the 0.80 threshold on 69.3%, identifying the omission rather than only withholding an answer. The secondary panel shows the same pattern with wider intervals (63.6% false resolution without the option, 6.1% with it, on the 33 questions with M≥3M\geq 3). The discovery runs of Section 5.2 elicit beliefs over the generated alternatives alone; this test holds the questions and evidence fixed and isolates what the added option does when an explanation is missing, not how it would change adaptive search or full-run yield. In those runs a missing alternative can force a wrong resolution only on a set that omits one, and two external checks show such sets are few: a strict majority of experts flagged a missing alternative on 6 of the 60 sets they rated, and on the 51 items our system resolved, experts preferred a competing explanation on only 1 (Appendix I).

Appendix L Baselines and Robustness of the Gain

This appendix gives the details behind Section 5.5. All analyses replay or re-score the logged discovery runs; none changes the resolution rules or the aggregation of the headline (within-run top-KK, seed mean within dataset, then mean over the six datasets).

Matched budgets.

Every run logs the cost of each individual candidate. Within each of the 14 matched dataset/seed pairs we capped both methods at the smaller of the two methods’ own totals in a given currency, walking candidates in the order they were produced and charging every one, including failed or unusable attempts, until the run reached its 200 experimental validations. Under equal total tokens the methods reached 181 (pointwise) and 189 (Contrastive) of their 200 scored candidates and resolved 87.7 against 148.3 units (difference +60.7+60.7, 95% tt interval over six dataset clusters [+23.4,+98.0][+23.4,+98.0]); under equal logged dollars, 92.2 against 145.8 ([+22.4,+84.8][+22.4,+84.8]); charging output tokens only, 95.8 against 124.9 ([−0.9,+59.1][-0.9,+59.1], the one interval that includes zero; five of six datasets positive). Applying one common budget to every run (4.45M tokens, the smallest total that any run spent) gives 52.4 against 89.6. Belief elicitation accounts for 8.5% of contrastive tokens against 2.5% for pointwise, but total spend per candidate is similar (61.1k tokens for pointwise against 52.8k for Contrastive), because the extra cost of writing the contrast set is offset by shorter analysis code and interpretation; since the cap charges failed and unusable attempts as well, the method with the cheaper candidate does not necessarily reach more scored ones. We do not read this as an efficiency advantage, since the two methods differ in prompts throughout and a token count cannot tell a narrower experiment from a thinner one.

Joint versus independent scoring.

Every contrast set in our runs was also scored one alternative at a time with the pointwise elicitor (five-level categorical rating mapped to a Beta mean, ten samples), never mentioning the other alternatives; the independent scoring additionally saw the experiment-reviewer agent’s notes, so the comparison is conservative against joint scoring. Applying the pointwise method’s own gate (γsupport=0.625\gamma_{\mathrm{support}}=0.625) to the independent scores under the paper’s estimator gives 157.8 resolved units at top-200 when exactly one alternative passes (165.4 when any passes), against 161.9 for joint scoring: a difference of 4.1 units, about 6% of the 64.7-unit headline gap, with a tt interval that includes zero. The two scorings name the same leading alternative on 89.3% of sets under dataset-equal weighting, and against the 170 questions with a statistic recomputed from raw data neither is more accurate (166 against 165 of 170). We therefore claim no advantage for scoring the alternatives together: given a fixed contrast set and its evidence, the scoring format accounts for a small share of the gap. Both scorings read the same analyst summary, so this check holds the analyst fixed. That resolutions follow the evidence rather than the analyst’s framing is established separately: the elicitor resolves from the numbers alone with no analyst (Appendix J), and experts who read the same evidence with no instruction chose the same explanation on 78% of resolved items (Appendix I). What remains is how the alternatives are constructed, tested directly below.

Implicit contrast sets in the pointwise corpus.

Could the pointwise runs’ hypotheses be clustered post hoc into the contrast sets we construct explicitly? Coverage is a necessary condition for such clustering: every member of a set must have been proposed. We screened every hypothesis generated by the pointwise runs (8,547 hypotheses over 32 runs) against a stratified sample of 300 contrast sets from the same datasets, judging each candidate pair with a model that generated neither corpus (gpt-4.1-mini) under a rubric that permits refusal. The matcher assigns a set’s own alternatives to the correct member on 99.9% of positive controls and matches nothing from unrelated datasets; blinded human labels on 40 matcher decisions agreed on 36, with three of the four disagreements being matches the human rejected, so the matcher errs toward overcounting pointwise coverage. At matched budget (the same-seed pointwise run truncated at the paired contrastive run’s total tokens), 29.1% of individual alternatives appear anywhere in the pointwise corpus, the runs share at least one alternative with 64.7% of the sets, and the complete set is present for 2.6% of the questions that at least one pointwise hypothesis addresses (95% tt interval [0,7.0][0,7.0], truncated at zero). Enlarging the corpus to all seeds and prompt variants, four to six times the matched budget, raises complete-set presence only to 15.4% ([0,31.5][0,31.5], wide) and per-alternative coverage to 53.7%. The explanation that the evidence eventually supports is present 52.0% of the time when it confirms the prior-leading explanation but 25.4% when it corrects it (paired difference −26.5-26.5 percentage points, [−44.8,−8.3][-44.8,-8.3]), so exactly where pointwise evaluation rejects its hypothesis and stops, its corpus usually lacks the explanation that turns out to hold.

Sensitivity to the number of alternatives.

Stratifying the frozen top-200 pool of Section 5.2 by contrast-set size, resolution is 93.4% with two alternatives (102 questions, 4.4% of validations, dataset-weighted), 83.2% with three (2,217; 78.3%), and 68.3% with four (479; 17.3%). Resolution requires 80% of posterior mass on one alternative however many are on the table, and belief starts more spread out with four alternatives (leading prior mass 0.41) than with two (0.68), so the bar is a longer climb; the evidence itself is not weaker on larger sets, where raw belief change rises from 0.59 to 1.07 bits. The number of alternatives was chosen by the generator and is confounded with question type: directional questions are almost all three-way and resolve at 92.7%, and a separate pooled comparison gives a three-to-four gap of 15.7 percentage points, which shrinks to 2.2 after standardizing the question types represented in both strata to the four-way mix. On paired support-scope questions the pointwise gate fires 12.2 percentage points more often than ours where there are four alternatives, so there is no evidence that our threshold becomes the more permissive one as contrast sets grow. This series covers two to four alternatives, excluding one five-way and one seven-way question, and describes how resolution varies with MM; it does not isolate a causal effect of MM.

Elicitation format.

On the same 180 contrast sets and byte-identical evidence, we re-elicited beliefs under two other response formats: a per-alternative five-level categorical judgment (the pointwise scoring rule) and a forced choice among the alternatives with the option that the evidence does not distinguish them. Among sets yielding a comparable decision, the leading explanation agreed with the paper’s 100-point allocation on 94.2% of sets under the categorical format (161 of 171) and 99.3% under forced choice (152 of 153), against 98.9% when the paper’s own format was run twice; before the evidence the formats agree only 57.1% and 76.8%, so the post-evidence agreement comes from the evidence rather than from the formats tracking one another. These figures hold for the canonical cell display used in the runs; the categorical format sits 4.7 percentage points below the repeatability ceiling, so the claim is agreement on the leading explanation rather than full format invariance.

Appendix M Exploration Breadth: Column Coverage and Sibling Anchoring

M.1 Results

We characterize the breadth with which each method explores the dataset’s variable space during hypothesis generation. For each generated hypothesis we extract the set of dataset columns it references via a lexical pipeline that combines signals from the executed code, the experiment plan, and the agent’s analysis. Letting CiC_{i} denote the canonical columns referenced by hypothesis ii and CC the dataset’s total column count, we define cumulative column coverage Coverage⁡(t)=|⋃i≤tCi|/C\mathrm{Coverage}(t)=|\bigcup_{i\leq t}C_{i}|/C and summarize each trajectory with a two-parameter saturating-exponential fit Coverage⁡(t)=α⁡(1−e−k​t)\mathrm{Coverage}(t)=\alpha(1-e^{-kt}), where α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] is the asymptotic coverage fraction and k>0k>0 is the rate constant; this is the rank-1 summary of a biased coupon-collector process in which high-salience columns are sampled more frequently than low-salience ones.

Figure 7, Figure 8 and Table 11 report the fits across our six datasets. On four of six datasets both methods reach high asymptotic coverage (α>0.9\alpha>0.9), and pointwise reaches a higher asymptote than Contrastive on five of six. Requirements Engineering has the lowest coverage, with fitted asymptotes of α=0.513\alpha=0.513 for pointwise and α=0.411\alpha=0.411 for Contrastive: about half of its columns are never touched by either method, however many hypotheses are proposed. Figure 9 and Table 12 compare column overlap between sibling and non-sibling nodes.

M.2 Extraction

For each generated hypothesis, we extract the set of dataset columns it references by parsing four fields from the run logs: the hypothesis text, the agent’s experiment plan (objective, steps, deliverables), the executed Python code, and the agent’s textual analysis. We use four lexical signals to identify column references: an AST parse of the executed code to detect pandas-style column accesses (e.g., df[’col’]), a regex fallback for cases where the code fails to parse, identifier tokenization on statsmodels-style formula strings, and substring matching of canonical column names against the concatenated textual fields. Each candidate token is validated against the dataset’s canonical column list (parsed from the run’s data-loading description) and dropped if it does not match a known column. The pipeline is fully lexical and uses no LLM calls.

M.3 Cumulative coverage and saturation fit

Given per-hypothesis touched-sets {Ci}i=1T\{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T} for a single run of TT hypotheses, we define cumulative coverage as

U⁡(t)=|⋃i=1tCi|,Coverage⁡(t)=U⁡(t)/C∈[0,1],U(t)=\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{t}C_{i}\right|,\qquad\mathrm{Coverage}(t)=U(t)/C\in[0,1], (5)

where CC is the dataset’s column count. We summarize each trajectory with a two-parameter saturating exponential fit

Coverage⁡(t)=α⁡(1−e−k​t),\mathrm{Coverage}(t)=\alpha\,(1-e^{-kt}), (6)

where α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] is the asymptotic coverage fraction and k>0k>0 is the rate constant. Fitting is performed by nonlinear least squares against the order-independent permuted-mean coverage curve (averaged over 20 random orderings of the hypotheses).

M.4 Limitations

The lexical pipeline cannot distinguish between hypotheses that touch the same columns through different mechanisms; an additional semantic-tagging layer would be required for that distinction and is left for future work. All results in this section reflect a single seed per (dataset, condition) cell and are presented as descriptive characterization rather than as statistical tests.

Appendix N Recovery of Published Findings

We screened 14 questions with published findings from the DiscoveryBench [32] training split and tested recovery on ten leakage-screened questions (questions whose wording gives away the answer were excluded). Each method received the question and the data once, with no tree search and never the answer, and the final hypothesis each run stated was scored against the published answer by a calibrated judge (gpt-4.1, temperature 0, 9 of 9 on calibration items), with undecided or malformed outputs counted as wrong. Contrastive Discovery matched on 1 of 10 and the pointwise baseline on 0 of 10. The transcripts show why: the analyst usually answered a different question than the benchmark asked (a different predictor or outcome, an unrequested moderator or subgroup), and several published answers depend on modeling choices of the original studies that cannot be recovered from the question and column schema. The test therefore measures question framing and analysis choice at least as much as adjudication, and with both methods at floor it says nothing about the difference between them. The correctness evidence in this paper comes instead from Appendix I and Appendix J, which start from the executed analysis; end-to-end recovery of known findings from raw data remains open.

Appendix O Elicitation Design Across the Two Methods

The pointwise and Contrastive methods share the discovery scaffold but differ in how beliefs are elicited and in what the analyst is asked to report. We list the main differences here, with what has been tested about each.

  • •

    Response format and aggregation. Pointwise beliefs are five-level categorical ratings (ten samples) mapped to a Beta mean (Appendix ); Contrastive beliefs are 100-point constant-sum allocations (five samples) averaged into a distribution (Appendix ). Scoring the same contrast sets one alternative at a time with the pointwise format changes the leading explanation on about one set in ten (89.3% agreement) and the headline by 4.1 resolved units (Appendix L); a per-alternative categorical format and a forced choice reproduce the leading explanation on 94.2% and 99.3% of sets yielding comparable decisions (Appendix L).

  • •

    Elicitor instructions. The Contrastive prior prompt asks the elicitor not to default to a uniform allocation, and the Contrastive posterior prompt asks it to be discriminative and avoid unjustified hedging (Appendix P); the pointwise elicitor prompt has no corresponding instruction. Because resolution is read off the posterior, these instructions could raise the resolution rate on their own. Two checks bound this. On the resolution rate, the independent-scoring check of Appendix L keeps the contrast sets and evidence fixed and replaces our elicitor with the pointwise elicitor and its threshold, which carry no such instruction: the yield falls from 161.9 to 157.8 questions, about 4 of the 64.7 gained over pointwise. On the leading explanation, the expert panel of Appendix I, reading the same evidence with no instruction, selected the system’s leading explanation on 40 of 51 resolved items. The first check replaces the instructions and the response format together, so the 4.1 questions bound their combined effect. The gain over pointwise therefore does not rest on the elicitor being told to be discriminative.

  • •

    What the analyst reports. The Contrastive analyst returns a winning_cell_idx field and describes, by content rather than label, which alternatives the evidence does and does not rule out; the posterior elicitor then reads the analyst’s prose. The pointwise analyst writes a free summary of the code output. The adjudication-fidelity experiment (Appendix J) removes the analyst entirely, giving the elicitor the numbers alone, and still finds evidence-driven resolutions, while the mechanical audits confirm that the summaries quote the printed numbers; isolating the verdict field’s own effect on the discovery runs is left to future work.

  • •

    When alternatives are generated. In the discovery runs the contrast set is part of the experiment proposal and is fixed before the experiment runs, so the alternatives are named before any evidence exists. The post-hoc companion of Section 5.1 generates its alternatives from the hypothesis under test, the dataset’s variables, and the same earlier context a live proposer would have; the current analysis, its output, and the verdict on the hypothesis are withheld, and the companion is applied whether the hypothesis was confirmed or rejected.

  • •

    Review and revision. The Contrastive experiment-reviewer agent additionally flags whether an experiment discriminates among the alternatives and the reviser agent can rework a non-discriminating plan; the pointwise reviewer agent checks faithful implementation and whether the focal hypothesis was sufficiently tested. This is part of the contrastive method rather than a scoring artifact, and its cost is included in the matched-budget comparison (Appendix L).

  • •

    Normalization. Pointwise surprisal is normalized by an achievable ceiling derived from the prior (Appendix ), whereas κt\kappa_{t} is scaled by the constant log2⁡M\log_{2}M (Appendix ); the consequences of each are discussed where they are defined.

Appendix P Prompts

P.1 Contrastive Discovery-specific prompts

⬇
You are a research scientist doing open-ended, data-driven research using the provided dataset(s). Each step in your investigation, you must propose a CONTRAST SET of competing explanations rather than a single hypothesis, and an EXPERIMENT PLAN that DISCRIMINATES between them.
A contrast set is a small, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) partition of outcomes. Four operational requirements (all mandatory):
1. **Single local question.** All cells must answer ONE specific question (e.g. "what is the direction/presence/moderation structure of X->Y?"). Do not mix questions.
2. **Single variable set.** All cells reference the same target and predictor variables. Do not switch what is being measured.
3. **Single analysis family.** A single coherent analysis (one regression, one stratified test, one comparison) must plausibly distinguish among all cells. Avoid contrast sets where one cell needs regression, another needs clustering, and another needs causal discovery.
4. **Small discrete outcome space.** Prefer M=3. Use M=4 only when subgroup or mechanism structure genuinely requires it. M=5 should be rare.
Most contrast sets should include a residual cell ("no effect" / "no clear pattern" / "neither") so exhaustivity is real, not aspirational. Some partition families (SIGN, PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION, FEATURE_DOMINANCE) already include one by construction; do NOT add a second residual cell when the family already provides one. Uncertainty lives in the probability allocation downstream, not as a separate "we don’t know" cell inside the partition.
NAMED PARTITIONING DIMENSIONS (pick exactly ONE per contrast set):
- **SIGN** (M=3): {{positive effect, no effect, negative effect}} for a scalar relationship between two variables.
- **PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION** (M=3): {{effect absent, effect present positive, effect present negative}}. Use when sign is hard to commit to but presence/absence is.
- **SUBGROUP_MODERATED** (M=4): {{effect only in A, only in B, in both, in neither}} for a binary moderator.
- **MECHANISM_DISCRIMINATING** (M=3 or 4): {{association persists after controlling for C, association attenuates after controlling for C, association disappears (no residual effect after controls), no effect}}. Strictly OBSERVATIONAL wording – describe what regression coefficients DO under control adjustment, not WHY. Do NOT use mediation language ("X is mediated through M"); mediation is a causal-identification claim our designs do not support. Do NOT use "causes" / "causal pathway" language.
- **FUNCTIONAL_FORM** (M=3 or 4): {{linear positive, linear negative, nonlinear or threshold, no effect}}. Use only when the question is genuinely about the shape of the relationship AND sample size supports the distinction (e.g. n > 200 for a polynomial-vs-linear comparison; nonlinear claims need enough power to reject a linear null). Otherwise default to SIGN or PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION.
- **COARSE_ORDER** (M=3 or 4): coarse ordinal contrasts only – e.g. {{highest in A, highest in B, no clear ordering}}, or {{monotone increasing, monotone decreasing, non-monotone}}. NEVER enumerate full permutations like (A>B>C>D); coarsen those to one of the forms above.
- **VARIANCE_DIFFERENCE** (M=3): {{variance higher in subgroup A than B, variance higher in B than A, no significant difference in variance}} for second-moment / dispersion / heteroskedasticity questions. Distinct from SUBGROUP_MODERATED, which is about mean/effect differences. Use when the question is genuinely about how spread (variance, IQR, MAD) differs across groups, not how means do.
- **FEATURE_DOMINANCE** (M=3 or 4): {{feature X is the dominant predictor of outcome Z, feature Y is the dominant predictor, both contribute comparably, neither contributes meaningfully}} for multi-feature contribution decomposition. Distinct from SIGN (which concerns one relationship’s direction). Use when the question is which of several candidate predictors carries the signal.
EXTENDING THE TAXONOMY (last resort): if your question’s structure genuinely fits none of the named dimensions above – for example, a regime-change / threshold-effect question that FUNCTIONAL_FORM doesn’t cover, an interaction-structure question SUBGROUP_MODERATED can’t express, or some other genuinely novel structural shape – you may coin a new dimension. Name it in your own SHOUT_CASE in the ‘partitioning_dimension‘ field, and ensure cells satisfy the same MECE / falsifiability / mechanical-cell-mapping properties as the named dimensions (every cell must be a discrete observable pattern that the experiment plan’s analysis maps to mechanically). Inventing a new dimension is rare; the named ones cover the vast majority of cases. Prefer the named ones whenever they fit.
HARD CONSTRAINTS:
1. M <= 5. Never enumerate combinatorial outcome spaces (every ordering of several items, or every combination of several multi-valued outcomes).
2. Each cell is a complete falsifiable claim referencing the actual variable names – not a label like "positive" or "ordering A > B".
3. Pick exactly ONE partitioning dimension per contrast set (a named one when applicable; a coined one only when none of the named dimensions fits).
4. The experiment plan must produce an output that maps each cell to a specific quantitative criterion (e.g. "CI entirely above 0 -> C_1; contains 0 -> C_2; entirely below 0 -> C_3").
5. **Cells must differ in substantive statistical pattern** – sign, presence, subgroup membership, mechanism class, functional form, or coarse ordering. Cells that differ only in wording strength ("weak positive" vs "strong positive") are NOT a valid contrast – that is one hypothesis re-described, not multiple alternatives.
6. **Adequate support.** Do not define cells over sparse categories or tiny subgroups unless the experiment plan explicitly checks for adequate sample size (e.g. minimum n per cell, robustness checks, or power-aware test selection).
Example of a well-formed contrast set output (note that ‘cells‘ are PLAIN-CONTENT strings – the slot labels ‘C_1‘/‘C_2‘/‘C_3‘ belong only in the ‘experiment_plan.deliverables‘ cell-mapping criterion, not in the cell text):
“‘
cells:
- "Total citations increase with years since PhD"
- "No effect of years since PhD on total citations"
- "Total citations decrease with years since PhD"
partitioning_dimension: "SIGN"
rationale: "Test the direction of the citation-experience relationship; the residual cell covers no-effect."
experiment_plan:
objective: "Quantify the relationship between years-since-PhD and total citations."
steps: "Compute Spearman correlation between years_from_PhD and total_citations; report the 95% bootstrap CI."
deliverables: "Spearman rho + 95% bootstrap CI; cell-mapping is: CI entirely above 0 -> C_1; CI contains 0 -> C_2; CI entirely below 0 -> C_3."
“‘
Examples of well-formed discriminating plans:
- SIGN: "Compute Spearman correlation between X and Y with 95% bootstrap CI. Report the CI; the cell-mapping is: CI entirely above 0 -> C_1; CI contains 0 -> C_2; CI entirely below 0 -> C_3."
- SUBGROUP_MODERATED: "Fit interaction model Y ~ X * Z; test simple slopes of X within each level of Z; classify by which simple slopes are significant at alpha=0.05."
- FUNCTIONAL_FORM: "Fit linear and natural-spline models, compare BIC; if linear wins and slope CI excludes 0, classify by sign; otherwise use the spline residual structure to distinguish nonlinear from null."
Self-check before output:
(a) Count cells. M <= 5? Prefer M=3?
(b) Pick any two cells. Could BOTH be true on the same dataset? If yes, fix.
(c) Imagine 5 plausible experimental outcomes. Does each map to exactly one cell? If not, add a residual cell or coarsen.
(d) Does the plan output a quantity that can be cleanly mapped to a specific cell?
(e) Could ONE coherent analysis (regression / stratified comparison / model-comparison test) discriminate all cells? If not, the contrast spans too many questions; split it.
Other instructions you must follow:
1. Strictly use only the dataset(s) provided. Do not simulate dummy/synthetic data or columns that cannot be derived from existing columns.
2. Each contrast set should be creative, independent, and self-contained.
3. Use prior explorations as inspiration; do not repeat the same partition.
4. Multiple datasets: if provided, you may propose contrast sets that join across datasets.
The unit of discovery is the redistribution of belief across the cells of the contrast set after evidence – not the survival of a single claim. A good contrast set + discriminating plan moves probability mass between cells; a bad one leaves the prior untouched.
Now generate exactly {branching_factor} new contrast sets with their discriminating experiment plans.
⬇
You are a research scientist evaluating the code execution output for a contrastive scientific experiment. The experiment was designed to discriminate between the cells of a CONTRAST SET – a small mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive partition of outcomes (cells C_1, C_2, … given to you in the user message). Your job has two INDEPENDENT parts.
PART 1 – execution status (separate from whether the experiment discriminated):
Set ‘success=false‘ ONLY when the code itself failed:
- no code was executed
- the code raised an error
- the code’s first line contains ‘# [debug]‘ (debugging protocol – return success=false, note the debug execution, ask for the experiment to be retried)
- the code "failed silently": produced no interpretable quantitative output, no statistics relevant to the contrast set, only plots / log spam / unusable text
Otherwise, set ‘success=true‘. The code ran AND produced usable output. **This holds even if the experiment failed to discriminate among the cells** – that judgment belongs to the reviewer’s separate ‘discriminates‘ flag, not yours.
When success=true, write a short analysis summary: report the **main decision-relevant quantities** the code actually produced – effect estimates, CIs, p-values, model-comparison metrics, whichever the experiment computed – plus any caveats (sample size, missing data, sparse subgroups, etc.). Do NOT force a p-value if none was computed.
PART 2 – contrast-set mapping (independent of PART 1’s success flag):
Identify which cell of the contrast set is best supported by the experimental output. Use **only what the code output reports** – no prior expectations, no domain knowledge beyond the printed statistics. Return:
- ‘winning_cell_idx‘: zero-based index of the cell the evidence most cleanly favors.
- If the result decisively supports one cell (e.g. tight CI on one side, large effect with clear direction matching exactly one cell’s criterion), return that index.
- If the evidence is genuinely ambiguous between two or more cells (CI straddles boundaries, mixed signals, the planned cell-mapping criterion wasn’t actually computed), return **null**.
‘winning_cell_idx=null‘ is a legitimate honest answer compatible with ‘success=true‘. **A success=true analysis with winning_cell_idx=null** is the right output when the code ran cleanly but the result didn’t actually distinguish among cells. Prefer null over overclaiming when evidence is borderline.
In the analysis text, when discussing cells, **describe them by their content / semantics only – do NOT reference cells by their numerical label** (no "C_1", "C_2", etc.). For example, write "the evidence supports the effect-attenuates-after-controls scenario" rather than "the evidence supports C_2". The numerical labels are an artifact of how cells are presented to you in this specific prompt; downstream consumers (the posterior belief elicitor, auditors, future re-elicitations under different cell orderings) will see the cells in possibly different label positions, so a label like "C_2" written here will mislabel the cell in those contexts. The cell content / short description IS the cell’s identity; descriptions transfer correctly across orderings, labels do not. Briefly note which cells the evidence does and does not rule out (by description), and any reasons it may be ambiguous. Use ‘winning_cell_idx‘ to record the index – that field is reordered correctly downstream; the prose should be label-free.
⬇
You are a research scientist holistically reviewing a contrastive experiment pipeline: the generated code, the output, and the analysis against the original experiment plan AND the contrast set the experiment was meant to discriminate.
‘success=true‘ and ‘discriminates=true‘ are LOGICALLY INDEPENDENT. Judge each separately on the criteria below; do not let one bleed into the other.
Assess two things:
1. **Faithful implementation.** Was the experiment plan followed without significant deviation? Are the test, statistics, and reporting consistent with the plan? If you find code-level or pipeline-level issues (missing variables, wrong test, broken output), return ‘success=false‘ and explain.
2. **Discrimination.** Did the experiment, as implemented, produce evidence that meaningfully narrows the contrast set?
For the discrimination check, ask explicitly:
- **Did the implemented analysis actually compute the predeclared cell-mapping criterion?** The experiment plan should have named a specific criterion (e.g. "Spearman CI sign", "interaction p-value", "BIC delta between linear and spline"). If the code computed something else – even something interesting – ‘discriminates=false‘. The cells were defined relative to that criterion; an output that doesn’t map to the criterion can’t discriminate.
- **Did the evidence rule out at least one competing cell?** A plan that produces only a quantity consistent with one cell while leaving the others untouched isn’t really a discriminating experiment.
- **Discrimination does not require statistical significance per se.** It comes from whichever criterion the plan declared – effect estimates, confidence intervals, model-comparison metrics, p-values – whichever was the predeclared rule for mapping output to cells. Do NOT require ‘p < 0.05‘ unless that was the rule.
Set the ‘discriminates‘ flag accordingly:
- **‘true‘** if the output, under the predeclared decision rule, narrows the contrast set to one cell or a near-singleton subset (i.e. one cell strongly favored, the others materially ruled out or implausible).
- **‘false‘** if the experiment passed but the evidence is too weak, ambiguous, doesn’t compute the predeclared criterion, or is equally consistent with multiple cells.
In the feedback text, separate the failure modes explicitly when they apply:
- **Implementation issue:** name what was wrong with the code, data, or pipeline (only when ‘success=false‘).
- **Non-discrimination:** explain why the evidence didn’t narrow the partition, and briefly note **what would have been needed to discriminate** (e.g. "tighter CIs", "stratified test", "model comparison instead of single-coefficient test"). Used when ‘success=true, discriminates=false‘.
When both flags are true, provide a summary of the contrast set, the experiment, and the resulting evidence-to-cell mapping.
⬇
You are a research scientist revising a contrastive experiment that the reviewer flagged. The experiment proposes a contrast set (a small mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive partition of outcomes) plus an experiment plan that should discriminate between the cells.
Default behavior: **preserve the cells; revise only the experiment plan.** Move the target only when you must.
ANTI-PATTERNS YOU MUST AVOID
- **Do not tighten the cells after seeing the data.** The cells were declared BEFORE evidence; revising them now to better match the observed result is HARKing – paper-indefensible. Tightening is allowed ONLY when the reviewer explicitly identified the original partition as ill-posed.
- **Do not respond to weak evidence by inventing a more specific subgroup or mechanism** unless the reviewer explicitly requested repartitioning. "The effect was weak in general but appears in subgroup X" is a post-hoc move and is forbidden.
- **Do not invoke "more powerful test" reasoning** as a justification for changing the analysis. "More powerful" is statistical jargon that invites fishing. Frame revisions as "more APPROPRIATE test" or "more INFORMATIVE analysis" – and explain why.
The reviewer’s feedback usually falls into one of these categories. Apply the corresponding revision in priority order – change as little as possible:
- **Technical failure** (code error, data issue, runtime crash, debug-marked code): keep the cells exactly as they are. Revise the plan to fix the technical problem. Do NOT change the partition.
- **Plan didn’t discriminate** (‘discriminates=false‘ from the reviewer): keep the cells. Revise the plan in this priority order – try the cheapest fix first:
1. **Change the decision rule / estimand / comparison structure.** E.g. switch from coefficient sign to model-comparison metric; add a CI for the existing estimate; switch from two-sample t-test to interaction term; recast as ordering test.
2. **Tighten the analysis without changing what is measured.** E.g. add controls, stratify, use a robust estimator, fix specification errors, address sparse-cell concerns.
3. **Change variables** – only as a last resort, and only if the reviewer flagged the original variables as the problem.
- **Partition itself is ill-posed** – only in this case, revise the cells. Operational rule: revise cells when (a) the reviewer explicitly flagged a MECE violation (cells overlap, fail to cover the outcome space, or answer different questions), or (b) the cells are not empirically distinguishable under any reasonable single analysis. Stay within the same partitioning dimension if possible; coarsen rather than refine.
HARD CONSTRAINTS for the revised contrast set (if you change it):
- M <= 5, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.
- Each cell is a complete falsifiable claim with the actual variable names.
- Pick exactly ONE partitioning dimension. The named taxonomy is SIGN / PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION / SUBGROUP_MODERATED / MECHANISM_DISCRIMINATING / FUNCTIONAL_FORM / COARSE_ORDER / VARIANCE_DIFFERENCE / FEATURE_DOMINANCE. If the original partition coined a custom SHOUT_CASE dimension that genuinely fits the question and meets the MECE / falsifiability / mechanical-cell-mapping properties, preserving that coined dimension is acceptable.
- Most revised contrast sets should include a residual / null cell (no effect / no clear pattern) for practical exhaustivity. Some families (SIGN, PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION, FEATURE_DOMINANCE) include one by construction; do NOT add a second when the family already provides one. No "uncertain" cells.
The revised experiment plan must:
- Address the reviewer’s specific concerns.
- **Explicitly state the cell-mapping rule** – the predeclared mapping from possible outcomes to cells (e.g. "CI entirely above 0 -> C_1; CI contains 0 -> C_2; CI entirely below 0 -> C_3"). Do NOT just say "do regression and interpret coefficients"; the cell-mapping must be declared so the next reviewer can check whether the implementation followed it.
- Output a quantity that maps to a single cell of the contrast set under one coherent analysis.
- Use only the provided dataset; no synthetic data.
Do not provide code – explain the revised experiment in natural language for the programmer.
⬇
## system_prior
You are a senior scientist making a comparative judgment about a research question. You will be given a set of mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) claims that partition the outcome space – exactly one is true given the real data, and you must allocate your prior belief across them.
Use your domain knowledge. Allocate exactly 100 probability points across the cells, summing to exactly 100. The points represent your prior probability (in percent) that each cell is the true one.
Do NOT default to a uniform allocation. Many research questions have informative priors – make them. If you genuinely have no view, allocate uniformly, but only if so.
Briefly explain your allocation in the rationale.
## system_posterior
You are a senior scientist judging which cell of a partition is true given experimental evidence.
You will be shown:
(a) A MECE contrast set: cells C_1, …, C_M that exhaust the outcome space.
(b) Experimental evidence: the analysis report from running the experiment.
Allocate exactly 100 probability points across the cells, summing to exactly 100, reflecting your posterior belief that each cell is the true one given the evidence. Be discriminative – if the evidence strongly supports one cell, put most of the mass there. If the evidence is weak or ambiguous across multiple cells, distribute accordingly. Avoid unjustified hedging.
Briefly explain your allocation in the rationale.
## user_template_prior
Research question:
{seed_hypothesis}
Variables involved:
{variables}
Contrast set ({n_cells} cells):
{cells_block}
Allocate 100 prior probability points across these cells. Sum must equal 100.
## user_template_posterior
Research question:
{seed_hypothesis}
Variables involved:
{variables}
Contrast set ({n_cells} cells):
{cells_block}
Experimental evidence (analysis):
{evidence}
Allocate 100 posterior probability points across these cells given this evidence. Sum must equal 100.

P.2 Pointwise Discovery-specific prompts

⬇
You are a research scientist who is interested in doing open-ended, data-driven research using the provided dataset(s). {user_query}Be creative and think of new and interesting verifiable {hyp_word} and corresponding {exp_word}. The hypothesis should be a falsifiable statement that can be sufficiently tested by an experiment using the provided data. Explain in natural language what this experiment plan is so that a programmer can implement it (do not provide the code yourself). Remember, you are interested in open-ended research, so your proposals may be exploratory in nature and may have only an indirect connection to the previous explorations provided. Here are some instructions that you must follow:
1. Strictly use only the dataset(s) provided and do not simulate dummy/synthetic data or columns that cannot be derived from the existing columns.
2. Each hypothesis (and experiment plan) should be creative, independent, and self-contained.
3. Use the prior experiments/hypotheses as inspiration to think of interesting and creative new experiments/hypotheses. However, do not repeat the same experiments/hypotheses.
Here is a possible approach to coming up with a new hypothesis and experiment plan:
1. Find an interesting context: this could be a specific subset of the data. E.g., if the dataset has multiple categorical variables, you could split the data based on specific values of such variables, which would then allow you to validate a hypothesis in the specific contexts defined by the values of those variables.
2. Find interesting variables: these could be the columns in the dataset that you find interesting or relevant to the context. You are allowed and encouraged to create composite variables derived from the existing variables.
3. Find interesting relationships: these are interactions between the variables that you find interesting or relevant to the context. You are encouraged to propose experiments involving complex predictive or causal models.
4. You must require that your proposed hypotheses are verifiable using robust statistical tests. Remember, your programmer can install python packages via pip which can allow it to write code for complex statistical analyses.
5. Multiple datasets: If you are provided with more than one dataset, then try to also propose hypotheses that utilize contexts, variables, and relationships across datasets, e.g., this may involve using join or similar operations.
Generally, in typical data-driven research, you will need to explore and visualize the data for possible high-level insights, clean, transform, or derive new variables from the dataset to be suited for the investigation, deep-dive into specific parts of the data for fine-grained analysis, perform data modeling, and run statistical tests. Now, generate exactly {branching_factor} new hypotheses with their experiment plans.
⬇
You are a research scientist responsible for evaluating the code execution output for a scientific experiment written by a programmer. If no code was executed, there was an error, or the code fails silently, return the success status as **false**. If the code includes a line "# [debug]" i.e "[debug]" as a comment, strictly treat this as a debugging experiment. In such cases, strictly return the success status as **false**, provide information that it was a debug code execution, give feedback and request the experiment to be retried with the new information. Otherwise, analyze the results and provide a short summary of the code output.
⬇
You are a research scientist responsible for holistically reviewing the entire experiment pipeline, i.e., the generated code, the output, and the analysis w.r.t. the original experiment plan. Assess whether the experiment was faithfully implemented, i.e., whether the implementation follows the experiment plan without significant deviation and whether the hypothesis was in fact tested sufficiently. If you find issues or inconsistencies in any part of the experiment pipeline, return the success status as **false** and provide feedback about what is wrong. Otherwise, return the success status as **true** and provide a summary of the hypothesis, experiment results, and findings.
⬇
You are a research scientist revisiting the most recent experiment, which could not be conducted correctly due to issues in the code or the formulation of the experiment plan,as indicated by the reviewer. Your goal is to revise this failed experiment plan by addressing the issues and limitations pointed out by the reviewer. The revised experiment plan should still aim to validate the most recent hypothesis. Do not provide the code yourself but explain in natural language what the experiment should do for a programmer. Strictly use only the dataset provided and do not create synthetic data or columns that cannot be derived from the given columns. The experiment should be creative, independent, and self-contained. Generally, in typical data-driven research, you will need to explore and visualize the data for possible high-level insights, clean, transform, or derive new variables from the dataset to be suited for the investigation, deep-dive into specific parts of the data for fine-grained analysis, perform data modeling, and run statistical tests.
⬇
## system_base
You are a research scientist skilled at analyzing scientific hypotheses. Your task is to provide your belief about the given hypothesis.
## system_with_evidence
Use the provided evidence collected from running experiments to help make your decision. Carefully consider each piece of evidence and decide whether and how any of them affects your belief about the current hypothesis. Note that evidence from previous studies may have an indirect bearing on the hypothesis, so think about how they might relate to the hypothesis even if they do not directly test it.
## system_use_prior
Use your prior knowledge of the research domain to help in your assessment of the hypothesis.
## system_disregard_prior
Disregard any prior beliefs you have about the hypothesis and focus only on the provided evidence.
## user_template
Hypothesis: {hypothesis}
Carefully reason before making your assessment.
## user_template_with_evidence
Carefully reason before making your assessment.
## Response schema
The LLM is asked (via Pydantic-typed structured output) to return one of:
- ‘definitely_true‘ (score 1.00)
- ‘maybe_true‘ (score 0.75)
- ‘uncertain‘ (score 0.50)
- ‘maybe_false‘ (score 0.25)
- ‘definitely_false‘ (score 0.00)

P.3 Other prompts

⬇
You are a scientific experiment programmer proficient in writing python code given an experiment plan. Your code will be included in a python file that is executed and any relevant results should be printed to standard out or presented using plt.show appropriately. Make sure you provide python code in the proper format to execute. Ensure your code is clean and concise, and include debug statements only when they are absolutely necessary. Use only the dataset given and do not assume any other files are available. The state is not preserved between code blocks, so do not assume any variables or imports from previous code blocks. Import any libraries you need to use. Always attempt to import a library before installing it (it may already be installed). If you need to install a library, use the following code example:{install_snippet}When installing python packages, use the –quiet option to minimize unnecessary output.Prefer using installed libraries over installing new libraries whenever possible. If possible, instead of downgrading library versions, try to adapt your code to work with a more updated version that is already installed. Never attempt to create a new environment. Always use the current environment. If the code requires generating plots, use plt.show (not plt.savefig). Avoid printing the whole data structure to the console directly if it is large; instead, print concise results that are directly relevant to the experiment. You are allowed 6 total attempts to run the code, including debugging attempts.
Debugging instructions:
1. Only debug if you are either unsure about the executability or validity of the code (i.e., whether it satisfies the proposed experiment).
2. If the code you are writing is intended for debugging, the first line of your code must be "# [debug]" only.
3. DO NOT use "[debug]" anywhere else in your code.
4. DO NOT combine any debug code and the actual experiment implementation code; keep them separate.
5. For each experiment, you are allowed to debug at most 3 times.
6. As much as possible, minimize the number of debugging steps you use.
⬇
## system
You are a research scientist responsible for analyzing plots and figures from running experiments and providing detailed descriptions.
## user
Please analyze the given plot image and provide the following:
1. Plot Type: Identify the type of plot (e.g., heatmap, bar plot, scatter plot) and its purpose.
2. Axes:
* Titles and labels, including units.
* Value ranges for both axes.
3. Data Trends:
* For scatter plots: note trends, clusters, or outliers.
* For bar plots: highlight the tallest and shortest bars and patterns.
* For heatmaps: identify areas of high and low values.
etc…
4. Annotations and Legends: Describe key annotations or legends.
5. Statistical Insights: Provide insights based on the information presented in the plot.

# System message is identical to the hypothesis generator prompt
Generate exactly 1 contrast set under these PINNED-CELL rules:
PINNED CELL (must be C_1, verbatim):
{pinned_hypothesis_text}
REQUIRED: generate AT LEAST 2 alternative cells (C_2, C_3, and optionally C_4) so the contrast set has M=3 or M=4 in total. M=3 is the default (= pinned cell + your 2 alternatives) as required by your system prompt; choose M=4 only when the natural partitioning dimension is SUBGROUP_MODERATED, MECHANISM_DISCRIMINATING(M=4), FUNCTIONAL_FORM(M=4), or COARSE_ORDER(M=4). DO NOT return only 1 alternative – an M=2 contrast set is invalid (no M=2 family appears in your system prompt’s allowed partitioning dimensions). Your alternatives plus the pinned cell must form a valid MECE partition under one of: SIGN, PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION, SUBGROUP_MODERATED, MECHANISM_DISCRIMINATING, FUNCTIONAL_FORM, COARSE_ORDER – whichever fits the pinned cell’s framing.
Output the contrast set with the pinned cell as the FIRST entry of ‘cells‘. Cells C_2 … C_M are the alternatives you generated. The ‘experiment_plan‘ you emit will be discarded (the experiment already happened); focus the rationale on why these alternatives are the right MECE complement to C_1.
⬇
You are a scientific peer reviewer evaluating the novelty of a research hypothesis, judged against the existing body of scientific research and common knowledge.
Novelty also includes originality and innovativeness of the hypothesis.
Rate the hypothesis on a scale of 1-5:
1 - Not original. Closely resembles existing research or common knowledge with little to no innovation.
2 - Slightly original. Minor variation or incremental refinement of well-known ideas.
3 - Moderately original. Brings some new insights but largely follows well-established concepts or combines known ideas in a modest way.
4 - Highly original. Proposes a non-obvious relationship or mechanism that goes meaningfully beyond existing work.
5 - Extremely novel and groundbreaking. Introduces a creative, surprising, or counterintuitive idea that could shift thinking in the field.
Focus on the scientific content of the hypothesis itself, not the writing quality, and do not reward vagueness.

Rate the hypothesis on a scale of 1-5:

Appendix Q Extended Results

Q.1 Per-dataset breakdown for Section 5.1

Refer to Figure 10, Figure 11, and Figure 12 for a per-dataset breakdown. Counts are averaged over runs, so the nn under each dataset is the mean number of nodes per run, shown to one decimal where the mean is fractional; the pooled column sums the six per-dataset means.

Q.2 Ruled-out alternatives (companion to Figure 3)

The same contrastive update that resolves a question also rules out competing alternatives, so the count of ruled-out alternatives rises with resolution. Figure 13 is a by-product of Figure 3 rather than an independent yield. Take, for example, a contrast set of three alternatives. A resolved set (maxm⁡pt,mpost≥0.80\max_{m}p^{\text{post}}_{t,m}\geq 0.80) leaves at most 0.200.20 for the two remaining alternatives, so at least one of them is at most 0.100.10 by construction, and is ruled out (p<τreject=0.10p<\tau_{\mathrm{reject}}=0.10) unless the two split the remainder exactly evenly. The Contrastive curve counts questions with at least one ruled-out alternative, and each pointwise curve counts rejected hypotheses; bands are ±1\pm 1 standard error across datasets.

In pointwise discovery, a candidate can only be confirmed, rejected, or left ambiguous; in Contrastive Discovery, the same evidence is distributed across a local partition, so one explanation can become strongly supported while others are simultaneously ruled out. Ruling out alternatives is thus not a competing outcome, but a by-product of successful contrastive resolution.

Both the curves in Figure 3 and Figure 13 are means over datasets and bands are ±1\pm 1 standard error across the six datasets.

Q.3 Decisive-unit and winner-switch rates for Section 5.3

Refer to Figure 14 for decisive-unit rate and winner-switch rate. The decisive-unit rate is the fraction of top-KK units on which a method reached any verdict under its own gates: for pointwise, confirmed (μpost≥γsupport\mu^{\text{post}}\geq\gamma_{\mathrm{support}}) or rejected (μpost≤γreject\mu^{\text{post}}\leq\gamma_{\mathrm{reject}}); for Contrastive, resolved (maxm⁡pt,mpost≥τsupport\max_{m}p^{\text{post}}_{t,m}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{support}}) or at least one alternative ruled out (minm⁡pt,mpost<τreject\min_{m}p^{\text{post}}_{t,m}<\tau_{\mathrm{reject}}). It is the counterpart of the resolution rate in Figure 3 that counts a verdict in either direction for both methods: at K=200K=200, Full Contrastive reaches 0.91 against 0.82 for pointwise, and is higher in each of the six datasets.

Q.4 Selection-rule ablations for Appendix 

15(a) compares the Contrastive selection rules: cumulative pointwise-surprising findings when each contrast set is projected to a single member under a different rule. The highest-posterior rule, the explanation the system declares the winner, is the least surprising projection. This is expected: a resolved winner is by construction the alternative the evidence favors, so its confirmation registers little pointwise surprisal. It is the tension between resolution and surprise, not a contradiction of Appendix .

15(b)reports a structured pointwise-prompt ablation, in which the single-hypothesis generator receives a contrast-style prompt. On cumulative surprisal its curve sits visibly above the vanilla pointwise baseline; we did not run a statistical test on this difference, and the appropriate comparator on the Contrastive side is the random-projection curve of 15(a) (not the highest-prior projection), against which the variant shows no clear difference. Because it is reported on surprisal rather than on resolution, it does not bear on the headline comparison of Section 5.2; the headline comparison uses the standard pointwise baseline, and evaluating this variant on resolution is future work.
